::: {.lead}
Today you put the sales of one week in order, like in a lab. Each
experiment has two parts. **Part A** is in Excel on the lab computer.
**Part B** is on a simulator of the interactive lesson: on paper, scan its
QR code; on the screen, click its link. After each step, write your result
in its box. At the end, copy your key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a computer with Excel (the desktop app, or Excel on the web
  at `office.com`) and the start file.
- **No lab computer today?** Your teacher does Part A on the screen, on the
  simulators of the interactive lesson. Do Part B on your phone.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. Look only after
  you try. On the interactive lesson, every step has a check that answers
  at once.

{{< start-files >}}

## Experiment 1 · Sort

**The idea:** **Sort** (Data › Sort) puts the rows of a table in order: by
a number (largest to smallest) or by a word (A to Z). Click **one cell** of
the table first: then each row moves as a whole. If you select one column
only, Excel shows a **Sort Warning**: choose *Expand the selection*, or the
totals leave their rows.

**Aim:** put the rows in order, and see that each row moves as a whole.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Excel)**
:::

1. Open `sales-start.xlsx`, sheet **Sales**. Click one cell of the table.
   Choose **Data › Sort**, sort by **Total (JD)**, order **Largest to
   Smallest**, and click OK.

   {{< record "On top: … ; at the bottom: …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   On top: the **bag of Wednesday, 48 JD**. At the bottom: the **water of
   Sunday, 9 JD**. Each row moved as a whole: the day and the item stayed
   with their total.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You sort by **Total (JD)**, largest to smallest. What is on top?

   - [x] the bag of Wednesday, 48 JD

     Why: The largest total comes first, with its whole row.

   - [ ] the water of Sunday, 9 JD

     Why: That is the smallest total: it goes to the bottom.

   - [ ] the first row of the table, as before

     Why: Sort changes the order of the rows.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="sims/table-lab.html" poster="sims/table-lab.png" title="Table Lab: sort, filter and colour the Sunrise sales" >}}

2. In **Table Lab**, do Task 1: sort the table by Total (JD), largest
   first. Which sale is on top?

   {{< record "On top in Table Lab: …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **The bag on Tuesday, 36 JD**; the juice on Sunday (10 JD) is at the
   bottom. (Table Lab has its own week of sales.)
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   Excel shows a **Sort Warning**. Safe or wrong? Sort the ways.

   Safe: each row stays whole
   :   Cancel, click one cell of the table, then sort.

       Why: Excel then sorts the whole table.

   :   Expand the selection.

       Why: The whole table is sorted, row by row.

   Wrong: the totals leave their rows
   :   Continue with the current selection.

       Why: Only one column moves: the totals no longer match their days and items.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · Filter

**The idea:** a **filter** (Data › Filter) shows only the rows that you need,
for example one type. The other rows are only **hidden**, never deleted:
**Clear Filter** brings them back. The status bar adds only the rows that
you see.

**Aim:** show only the rows that you need, and add them up.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Excel)**
:::

1. Click one cell of the table. Choose **Data › Filter**. Click the arrow
   of **Type**, tick only **Paper**, and click OK. Select the totals that
   you see and read **Sum** in the status bar. Then choose **Clear Filter
   From "Type"**.

   {{< record "Rows of Paper … ; Sum … ; after Clear Filter … rows" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **4 rows** (the pens and the notebooks), **Sum: 77** (15 + 30 + 12 +
   20). After Clear Filter, **all 10 rows** come back: a filter hides rows,
   it never deletes them.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="77" hint="15 + 30 + 12 + 20."}
   With only **Paper** ticked, what Sum does the status bar show for the
   four totals?

   Why: 15 + 30 + 12 + 20 = 77. The status bar adds only the rows that you see.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="sims/table-lab.html" poster="sims/table-lab.png" title="Table Lab: sort, filter and colour the Sunrise sales" >}}

2. In **Table Lab**, do Task 2: show only the rows of the type **Drinks**.
   How many rows stay?

   {{< record "Drinks: … rows ; their total … JD" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **4 rows**, with a total of **50 JD**. The other rows are hidden, not
   deleted.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You clear the filter. What happens to the hidden rows?

   - [x] They all come back.

     Why: A filter only hides rows.

   - [ ] They are gone.

     Why: A filter never deletes rows.

   - [ ] Only the filtered rows stay.

     Why: Clear Filter shows every row again.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · A colour rule

**The idea:** **conditional formatting** colours cells by a rule, for
example *Greater Than 20* (Home › Conditional Formatting › Highlight Cells
Rules). The rule checks the cells again when a number changes; a colour
that you add by hand does not.

**Aim:** colour cells by a rule, and see the colour follow the numbers.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Excel)**
:::

1. Select the totals **E2:E11**. Choose **Home › Conditional Formatting ›
   Highlight Cells Rules › Greater Than**, type **20**, choose a colour and
   click OK. Then change the juice of Tuesday (14 JD) to **22**, look at
   the cell, and press **Ctrl + Z**.

   {{< record "Cells with the colour … ; the cell with 22 …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Three cells: 24, 30 and 48.** The total **20** keeps no colour: 20 is
   not greater than 20. The juice with **22** gets the colour by itself:
   the rule checks the cells again.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   The rule is **Greater Than 20**. Which totals get the colour? Sort them.

   The colour
   :   48

       Why: 48 is greater than 20.

   :   30

       Why: 30 is greater than 20.

   :   24

       Why: 24 is greater than 20.

   No colour
   :   20

       Why: 20 is not greater than 20.

   :   9

       Why: 9 is smaller than 20.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="sims/table-lab.html" poster="sims/table-lab.png" title="Table Lab: sort, filter and colour the Sunrise sales" >}}

2. In **Table Lab**, do Task 3: show all types again, then highlight the
   totals greater than 20. How many totals are green?

   {{< record "Green totals: …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Three**: 24, 36 and 24 JD. A total of 20 stays white: 20 is not
   greater than 20.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="3" hint="Count the totals bigger than 20: 24, 36 and 24."}
   In Table Lab, how many totals are greater than 20?

   Why: 24, 36 and 24 are greater than 20; 20 itself is not.
   :::

## Experiment 4 · Charts

**The idea:** a chart shows numbers as a picture. A **column** chart compares
amounts; a **line** chart shows a change over time; a **pie** chart shows
the parts of one whole. Give every chart a real title that says what it
shows, never "Chart Title".

**Aim:** make the right chart for each question, with a real title.

::: {.part}
**Part A · In the app (Excel)**
:::

1. On the sheet **Types**, select **A1:B4**. Choose **Insert › Recommended
   Charts** and a **Clustered Column** chart. Click *Chart Title* and type a
   real title.

   {{< record "My title … ; the highest column …" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A real title says what the chart shows, for example "Sales by type in
   one week (JD)". The highest column is **Paper (77)**. Columns compare
   amounts.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Which chart title is a real title?

   - [x] Sales by type in one week (JD)

     Why: It says what the chart shows, and the unit.

   - [ ] Chart Title

     Why: That is the empty title that Excel puts first.

   - [ ] Chart 1

     Why: It says nothing about the numbers.
   :::

2. Click the chart. Choose **Chart Design › Change Chart Type › Pie**. Then
   click **+** next to the chart and tick **Data Labels**.

   {{< record "The three labels" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **77, 51 and 72**: the three parts of 200 JD. A pie shows the parts of
   one whole. Paper is the biggest part.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="200" unit="JD" hint="Add the three labels."}
   The three labels of the pie are 77, 51 and 72. What is the whole?

   Why: 77 + 51 + 72 = 200 JD: the whole week. A pie shows the parts of one whole.
   :::

::: {.part}
**Part B · On the simulator** (no computer? do it on your phone)
:::

{{< sim file="sims/chart-lab.html" poster="sims/chart-lab.png" title="Chart Lab: the right chart for the question" >}}

3. In **Chart Lab**, do the three tasks: compare the types, show how the
   sales change from Sunday to Thursday, and show the part of each type.
   Which chart did you choose for the change from Sunday to Thursday?

   {{< record "Sunday to Thursday: a … chart" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **A line chart**: it shows a change over time. The types get a column
   chart (compare) and a pie chart (the parts of 185 JD).
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   Which chart answers each question? Sort them.

   Column chart
   :   Which type sold the most?

       Why: Columns compare amounts.

   Line chart
   :   How did the sales change from Sunday to Thursday?

       Why: A line shows a change over time.

   Pie chart
   :   What part of the week's sales is each type?

       Why: A pie shows the parts of one whole.
   :::
